original_question: Let T be a rooted labelled tree with n parking spaces and let f be an n-mapping on [n]. For m drivers, write S(T, m) for the number of parking sequences that successfully park on T and S(f, m) for the analogous number for f. Is there a simple general characterization of the counting functions S(T, m) and S(f, m), rather than only case-by-case formulas or bounds?
target_in_paper: No exact match appears in arXiv:2505.15826, which is a 2025 survey on parking problems on random trees. Your draft instead matches the explicit open question in the earlier combinatorics source Parking functions for trees and mappings / Chapter 9 of Lackner's thesis: "Is it possible in general to give some \"simple characterization\" of the numbers S(T,m) and S(f,m)?"
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the relevant counting objects S(T,m) and S(f,m), the two combinatorial structures involved (rooted labelled trees and n-mappings), and the paper's real emphasis: moving beyond special-case formulas and coarse bounds toward a general/simple characterization. That is essentially the substance of the open question stated in the further-research discussion of the original combinatorics work on parking functions for trees and mappings. The main problem is that the supplied arXiv ID points to a different survey paper.
missing_details: The arXiv identifier is mismatched: arXiv:2505.15826 is a survey on random-tree parking phase transitions and open directions, whereas the draft matches the earlier paper/thesis question on exact counting for fixed trees and mappings.
The formal setup should specify 0 ≤ m ≤ n, T a rooted labelled tree of size n on vertex set [n], f:[n]→[n] an n-mapping, and S(T,m), S(f,m) as counts of parking sequences s∈[n]^m.

To be stand-alone, the parking rule should be stated: each driver starts at her preferred vertex and follows the unique outgoing edge toward the root (for trees) or along the functional digraph (for mappings) until the first free parking space is found; if no reachable free space exists, that driver fails.

The nearby context in the paper says that only general bounds/extremal cases and formulas for some simple classes are known, while the paper computes total counts Fn,m=∑_{T∈T_n}S(T,m) and Mn,m=∑_{f∈M_n}S(f,m) rather than a general formula for each fixed T or f.
Relabelling invariance should be made explicit: by Proposition 9.8, isomorphic trees or mappings have the same counts, so the question is really about characterization up to isomorphism type.
For trees, the paper already gives an equivalent success criterion (Lemma 9.7) via rooted-subtree inequalities; mentioning this sharpens the tree side of the question.
No ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree, nilpotency, or 'for all sufficiently large m' clause is involved here; this is a finite combinatorial counting problem.
refined_question: For integers n≥1 and 0≤m≤n, let T be a rooted labelled tree of size n on [n], and let f:[n]→[n] be an n-mapping. Write S(T,m) and S(f,m) for the numbers of sequences s∈[n]^m for which, under the tree/mapping parking procedure, all m drivers park successfully. Since these counts are invariant under relabelling, can one in general give a simple characterization of the numbers S(T,m) and S(f,m), beyond the general bounds, extremal cases, and explicit formulas known for only some simple classes of trees or mappings?
equivalent_formulation: For the tree case only, Lemma 9.7 shows that this is equivalently the problem of counting sequences s∈[n]^m such that |{k∈[m]: s_k∈T'}|≤|T'| for every subtree T' of T containing root(T).
justification: The supplied arXiv paper, 2505.15826, is a survey about parking on random trees, phase transitions near m≈n/2, and broader open directions, so it does not contain the fixed-(T,f) counting question in your draft. Your draft instead aligns almost verbatim with the open problem stated in the further-research section of the original combinatorics source on parking functions for trees and mappings. The surrounding Chapter 9 context is exactly what your draft alludes to: Section 9.2 defines S(f,m), states that no general enumeration formula is known for general f, proves relabelling invariance in Proposition 9.8, and gives only extremal tree bounds in Theorem 9.10. I therefore kept the question narrowly at that level of generality and added only the missing definitions needed to make it stand alone.
